Keep the server authoritative: clients request actions through Server RPCs, and the server validates them before it changes any state.
Prefer replicated properties with RepNotify to RPCs, use multicast RPCs sparingly, and make frequently called RPCs unreliable.
Reference assets that aren't always needed with soft references (`TSoftObjectPtr`, `TSoftClassPtr`), and load them asynchronously.
Profile early and often on the target hardware, with Unreal Insights.
Register the content you load on demand, such as levels and data assets, as primary assets with the Asset Manager, and use asset bundles to control which secondary assets load with them.
Turn content rules, such as naming conventions and size or performance budgets, into Data Validation rules, and run the `DataValidation` commandlet in CI.
Write automated tests with the Automation Test Framework, use Low-Level Tests for pure unit tests, and run both from the command line in CI.
Keep One File Per Actor on (the default with World Partition), so that several people can change actors in the same level at once.

Keep all user-facing text in `FText`, created from text properties in assets, `LOCTEXT` macros in C++ or String Tables, and build messages with `FText::Format` and its `plural`, `ordinal` and `gender` argument modifiers.
Never mutate props, including nested properties of object props: emit an event so that the parent changes its own state, or use `defineModel()` for two-way binding.
Write application components as Single-File Components with the Composition API and `<script setup>`.
Derive values with `computed`, keep computed getters free of side effects, and use watchers only for side effects in reaction to state changes.
Declare props and emitted events with types, such as `defineProps<Props>()`, and type-check `.vue` files in CI with `vue-tsc`.

Extract reusable stateful logic into composables: name them `useX`, accept refs or getters and read them with `toValue()`, return a plain object of refs, and call them synchronously in `<script setup>` or `setup()`.

In server-rendered apps, never keep user or request data in module-level state: create the app, router and stores for each request, and in Nuxt keep shared state in `useState` or Pinia, not in refs exported from a module.
Use Pinia for state that many components share, instead of hand-rolled global `reactive()` objects.
In Nuxt, load the data a page renders with `useFetch` or `useAsyncData`, keep `$fetch` for requests that user events trigger, and use `pick` or `transform` to keep only the fields the page renders.

Render the same output on the server and in the browser: use SSR-safe composables, keep browser-only code in `onMounted()` or `<ClientOnly>`, and don't render values that differ between the two, such as the current time.

Use server-side rendering or static generation, for example with Nuxt, when page load performance or SEO matters, and a client-side SPA only when they don't. In Nuxt, set the rendering mode per route with `routeRules`.
Lazy-load route components with dynamic imports.
After each route change, move focus back to the start of the page, just before a skip link to the main content.
Never use untrusted content as a Vue template, and never mount Vue on server-rendered HTML that contains user-provided content.
Give an environment variable the `VITE_` prefix, or put a value in Nuxt's `runtimeConfig.public`, only if it may be public.
Run unit and component tests with Vitest, give each component its own component test, and in those tests interact with the component as a user would instead of mocking its child components.
Target WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the minimum for every page and component.
Use native HTML elements, such as `button`, `a`, `input` and `select`, before ARIA.
Run automated accessibility checks in CI, and also test by hand with a keyboard and a screen reader.
Measure Core Web Vitals from real users at the 75th percentile, separately for mobile and desktop, and set priorities from that field data.
Ship less JavaScript: split off code that the first render doesn't need, remove unused code, and use Baseline platform features instead of JavaScript reimplementations.
Give every image and embed explicit dimensions, offer sizes that fit the layout with `srcset` and `sizes`, and lazy-load only images outside the initial viewport.

Put a content hash or version in the URLs of static assets and cache them for a long time with `immutable`, and serve HTML with `Cache-Control: no-cache` (plus `private` when it's personalised) so that it's always revalidated.

Render untrusted data through the framework's automatic escaping or `textContent`, and sanitize it with DOMPurify before it reaches an HTML sink such as `innerHTML` or React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
Send security headers with every response: `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a `Referrer-Policy`, and the CSP `frame-ancestors` directive against framing.
Add a strict, nonce- or hash-based Content Security Policy as a second layer of defence against XSS, and try it in `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` mode before enforcing it.
Load third-party scripts with Subresource Integrity, or serve your own reviewed copies.
Choose a Baseline target, such as Baseline Widely available, from your users' browser data, and set it once in Browserslist so that build and lint tools share it.
Build core user journeys with progressive enhancement: HTML that works on its own first, then CSS and JavaScript that enhance it, so that a script that fails to load doesn't stop users.
Find elements in tests the way users find them: by role and accessible name first, then by label or text, and by test ID only when nothing visible identifies the element.

Never wait for a fixed time in a test: use actions that wait automatically and assertions that retry until the page reaches the expected state, such as Playwright's `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()` or Testing Library's `findBy` queries.

Isolate every test: run it in a fresh browser context, let it build the state and data it needs instead of relying on earlier tests, and when tests change server-side state, give each parallel worker its own user account.
Run the end-to-end tests in CI on every pull request, in each browser engine you support, and keep a trace of every failure.
Treat a flaky test as a bug: quarantine it outside the blocking pipeline, file a bug for it, and fix it within a set time.
Test components in a real browser, for example with Vitest Browser Mode, and keep end-to-end tests to the few user journeys that carry the product's core value.
Mock HTTP at the network level, for example with Mock Service Worker, instead of mocking `fetch` or your API client modules, and make requests without a handler fail the test.

Keep visual comparison (screenshot) tests to a few stable pages and components, hide dynamic content such as dates, and create and compare the screenshots in the same environment, with the same operating system and browser versions.
